_about: Plain-language explanations for parents (P4). Written for this demo from public sources, mainly GreatSchools' ratings guide at https://www.greatschools.org/gk/ratings/. Draft: GreatSchools should review and replace these with its own content before real use.

terms.title: GreatSchools Summary Rating
terms.text: A score from 1 to 10 that sums up how well a school serves its students. It combines smaller ratings, such as test scores, student progress, college readiness and equity. Roughly: 1-4 is below average, 5-6 is average and 7-10 is above average. Ratings compare schools within the same state, so a 7 in one state isn't the same as a 7 in another. Many private schools have no rating because they don't share state test results.

terms.title: Test Score Rating
terms.text: Shows how students at the school did on state tests compared with other schools in the state. It tells you about achievement, but not how much students grew during the year.

terms.title: Student Progress Rating
terms.text: Shows how much students improved from one year to the next, compared with similar students elsewhere in the state. A school can have average test scores but strong progress, which means it is helping kids move forward.

terms.title: College Readiness Rating
terms.text: For high schools. Looks at things like graduation rates, college entrance exams and advanced classes to show how well a school prepares students for college.

terms.title: Equity Rating
terms.text: Shows how well a school serves students from low-income families and from different racial and ethnic groups, compared with other students. A high equity rating means those students do well at this school too.

terms.title: Community rating (stars)
terms.text: The average star rating (1 to 5) from reviews written by parents, students and staff. It reflects people's experiences, not test data, and older reviews may not describe the school today.

terms.title: Public school
terms.text: A free school paid for with tax money and run by the local school district. Most children are assigned a public school based on their home address.

terms.title: Charter school
terms.text: A free public school that is run independently from the school district, under a contract (a 'charter') with the state or district. Anyone can apply. If more families apply than there are seats, there is usually a lottery.

terms.title: Magnet school
terms.text: A free public school or program with a special focus, such as STEM, the arts or languages. It can draw students from across the district, and some have an application or lottery.

terms.title: Private school
terms.text: A school that charges tuition and is not run by the government. Private schools set their own admissions and curriculum. Scholarships or state programs may help pay tuition in some states.

terms.title: Microschool
terms.text: A very small school, often with a few dozen students or fewer in mixed-age groups. Microschools may meet in homes or community spaces and are usually private or part of homeschooling. Rules and oversight vary by state.

terms.title: CTE (Career and Technical Education)
terms.text: Classes that teach job skills alongside regular school subjects, like health care, building trades, computer science or culinary arts. Students can sometimes earn certificates or college credit before they graduate.

terms.title: STEM
terms.text: Science, Technology, Engineering and Math. A STEM school or program puts extra focus on these subjects, often with hands-on projects, robotics or coding. STEAM adds the Arts.

terms.title: IEP (Individualized Education Program)
terms.text: A written plan for a child with a disability who needs special education. Public schools must make the plan with the family and follow it. It lists the child's goals and the support, services and changes the school will provide.

terms.title: 504 plan
terms.text: A plan that gives a student with a disability changes in how they learn, such as extra test time or a seat near the teacher, so they can take part in regular classes. It's for students who don't need special education services but do need support.

terms.title: English learners (ELL / ESL)
terms.text: Students who are still learning English. Schools must help them learn English and keep up in other subjects. Some schools also offer dual-language programs, where classes are taught in two languages.

terms.title: Gifted and talented
terms.text: Programs for students who learn faster or need more challenge than the regular class gives them. How students qualify, often by testing or teacher referral, depends on the district.

terms.title: AP and IB courses
terms.text: College-level classes taken in high school. With a good score on the final exam, students can earn college credit. Dual enrollment means taking real college classes while still in high school.

terms.title: Student-teacher ratio
terms.text: The number of students for each teacher at the school. A lower number usually means more attention for each child, but it isn't exactly the same as class size.

terms.title: Attendance and chronic absence
terms.text: Chronic absence usually means a student missed 10% or more of the school year, about 18 days. Schools with many chronically absent students may have problems worth asking about.

terms.title: Education Savings Account (ESA)
terms.text: A state program that puts public money into an account parents control. They can spend it on approved costs like private school tuition, tutoring, therapy or learning materials. Who qualifies and how much you get depend on your state.

terms.title: School voucher
terms.text: A state program that uses public money to pay some or all of a child's private school tuition. Rules about who qualifies depend on your state.

terms.title: Tax-credit scholarship
terms.text: People or businesses donate to a nonprofit scholarship group and get a tax credit in return. The group gives scholarships that help families pay private school costs. A federal program starting in 2027 adds more of these; what's offered depends on your state.

terms.title: Open enrollment / school choice
terms.text: Rules that let families apply to a public school other than the one assigned by their address. Seats, deadlines and transportation vary by district, so check early.

terms.title: What the checks on each school mean
terms.text: Confirmed: the data shows the school meets this need, and the data is recent. Partial: it meets the need only partly, only reviews support it, or the data is old. Needs attention: the data says the school doesn't meet it, or something in the data looks wrong. Missing: we have no data, so ask the school.
